# Introduction



<!-- #endregion -->

<!-- #region id="4fAKI7AJibGi" -->
## Basal Ganglia in Action Selection
<!-- #endregion -->

<!-- #region id="ulTFlhzLibdd" -->
In the vast neuroscientific literature regarding the basal ganglia, there are certain reocurring themes, such as evaluation of utility (how much reward an action is worth), action selection (what to do next), pattern generation (i.e., motor control, language production). 

This is due to the observation that dysfunctions of the BG can lead to repetitive behaviors, or inappropriate action selection, as for example in the Tourette syndrome (for a startling example, [watch this video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M8clZP-PI2Y)).


It is commonly believed that the basal ganglia are also the main organ dealing with reward based learning, due to its profusion of dopaminergic neurons and neurons with dopamine receptors.

In this project we will dive into the anatomy, dynamics and theories of basal ganglia function. We will use a spiking neural model (via NENGO) that captures essential features of the basal ganglia's neuroanatomy, and is able to perform a fundamental set of computations attributed to the BG, including action evaluation, selection and action sequencing. We will develop a minimal example of an action sequencing problem and will discuss some of the issues of encoding action selection with spikes.


<!-- #endregion -->

<!-- #region id="8m7sf45eP9B4" -->
## Learning Objectives

- Know the basic anatomic connections of the BG.
- Learn how direct and indirect pathways can compete via spiking neurons.
- Learn how to represent abstract concepts in spiking neuronal populations (semantic pointer architecture).
- Relate the problem of action selection with that of action sequencing.

<!-- #region id="0SUHYKcw_xYI" -->
### Action Selection Problem

Before going into action selection, we have to be explicit by what we mean with "action". An action can be defined as **a meaningful set of behaviors**. By meaningful we mean they have a set of 'fulfilment criteria', that is, one knows what an action 'is for', and whether it accomplished its objective. In that sense, it is different than a 'muscle spasm', that moves limbs without purpose. 

In other words, in order to accomplish something, one executes an action. Complex goals often require complex action sequences 'a plan'.

**Action selection:** selecting certain actions and suppressing the others for appropriate behavior to occur (Gurney et al., 2001). 

**Action selection problem:** In a particular context, there could be multiple alternatives of actions to select/execute. However, we can only perform at most a small set of actions at the same time, and many actions cannot be achieved simultaneuosly (particularly if they share the same motor output).

Moreover, there could be actions that have similar importance (conflicting) . In the action problem we have to choose an action even if we cannot distinguish them by expected reward. Symmetry has to be broken! 


<!-- #endregion -->

<!-- #region id="osPIxeWI2O6o" -->
## Anatomy and Physiology of the BG
<!-- #endregion -->

<!-- #region id="gs1pQBz2gaUV" -->
  Basal Ganglia refers to subcortical structures in the limbic system  above the midbrain. These subcortical structures are: Caudate and Putamen (collectively called Striatum), Subthalamic Nucleus (STN), Globus Pallidus Internus (GPi) and Globus Pallidus Externus (GPe), Substantia nigra (Sn). The neurons found in Basal Ganglia are called medium spiny striatal neurons. These neurons are inhibitory neurons that use GABA neurotransmitter.  

  Striatum consists of dopamine receptors: D1 and D2. Since these two types of dopamine receptors have different connections within the Basal Ganglia structures, they are often differentiated in theoretical models as: Striatum D1 and Striatum D2. 

  Basal Ganglia has connections with different areas of the brain including: Thalamus, Somatosensory cortex, Motor cortex, Prefrontal cortex and other areas in the cortex.  That is why, it is often associated with multiple functions such as: motivational behavior, reinforcement learning, coordinating and initiating movement, and action selection. 
  Basal Ganglia receives its input from cortex via Striatum and Subthalamic Nucleus and it sends output via the Globus Pallidus Internus and Substantia Nigra.
  
<!-- #endregion -->

<!-- #region id="uIsF2iOz79wg" -->
**Striatum:** Striatum is one of the input nuclei of Basal Ganglia. It receives excitatory input from cortex. Striatum refers to caudate and putamen. It is colored in light blue in the picture below.

**Striatum D1:** part of the Striatum that has D1 type receptors. It has an inhibitory connection (through GABA) with GPi. 

**Striatum D2:** part of the Striatum that has D2 type receptors. It has an inhibitory connection (through GABA) with GPe. 

**Subthalamic Nucleus (STN):** STN is another input nuclei of Basal Ganglia, it receives excitatory input from cortex. STN has excitatory connections (through AMPA) with GPe and GPi. It is colored in red in the picture below.

**Globus Pallidus Externus (GPe):** GPe receives input from Striatum D2 and sends its output to both STN and GPi via inhibitory connections. It is colored in light purple in the picture below.

**Globus Pallidus Internus (GPi):** It is the output nuclei of Basal Ganglia, where the output is sent to Thalamus and then back to the Cortex. GPi receives inhibitory input from Striatum D1 and GPi as well as excitatory input from STN. It has inhibitory connection to Thalamus. It is colored in green in the picture below.


<!-- #endregion -->

## A Computational Model of the Basal Ganglia

### GPR Model (Gurney et al., 2001)

The theoretical model of Basal Ganglia created by Gurney, et al. (2001), assumes that each action has a  **salience** value (a scalar), which refers to the action's importance in the current context of an organism. The salience value would be presumably acquired via previous rewarding experiences. Decision behavior requires that the action with the highest salience value should be chosen, and other actions either suppressed (inhibitted) or ignored (inactivated). 

In their model, they define action as "behavioural expression determined by a specific population of cells within Basal Ganglia". Given a context, the BG populations must initiate motor actions by activating cortical and spinal chord targets.

To decide which action to select and which to inhibit, Gurney et al. (2001) interpreted the anatomical and physiological evidence as a competition between pathways in Basal Ganglia, where the saliency winner is translated into an action, with the competing actions being inhibited. 

The model consists of three main pathways that compete. These pathways are:

**Hyperdirect Pathway:** This pathway has the "global control effect". Glutamatergic excitation from cortical neurons arrive at the STN, which then excites both GPi and GPe.

**Direct Pathway :** The "selection pathway" -- where a specific cortical saliency excites striatum D1 neurons, which inhibits the GPi. The action is triggered via the disinhibition of thalamus. 

**Indirect Pathway:** This pathway is the "control pathway" which inhibits/suppresses an action of insufficient saliency. When cortical neurons excite striatal D2 neurons, they "disinhibit" STN via GPe. Similarly, the GPi neurons are also disinhibited (Direct pathway), although to a lesser degree.





<!-- #endregion -->

<!-- #region id="8VPwUW726fz9" -->
![bgnew.jpg](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
<!-- #endregion -->

<!-- #region id="cNUTXXqiMM7K" -->
####Parameters in the model

- $w_{s}$ = weight for the excitatory connection from cortex to 
Striatum D1 and D2
- $w_{t}$ = weight for excitatory connection from cortex to STN
- $w_{m}$ = weight for the inhibitory connection from STD1 to GPi and from STD2 to GPe
- $w_{g}$ = weight for inhibitory connection from GPe to STN
- $w_{p}$ = weight for the excitatory connection from STN to GPe and GPi.
- $w_{e}$ = weight for the inhibitory connection from GPe to GPi
- $l_{g}$ = Dopamine parameter in Striatum D1
- $l_{e}$ = Dopamine parameter in Striatum D2
- The model uses these weights in the connections between components (ensembles) of BG, and in the connections between Basal Ganglia, and the Cortex and Thalamus connections. 
- For the connection between Cortex and Striatum D1 and D2, they used the formula of modified afferent synaptic strength. 
  - For Cortex - Striatum D1 connection, this is: $w_{s}$ $x$ ($1$ $+$ $l_{g}$)
  - For Cortex - Striatum D2 connection, this is: $w_{s}$ $x$ ($1$ $-$ $l_{e}$)

<!-- #endregion -->

<!-- #region id="UfnLfgsU3FOv" -->
### How do these pathways compete to select or inhibit actions?
<!-- #endregion -->

<!-- #region id="LoOUvQ_y6L0d" -->
Input coming from the cortex consists of salience values for action options. This input is sent to the input nuclei of Basal Ganglia: Striatum and Subthalamic Nucleus via excitatory connections. 


When dopaminergic medium spiny neurons in Striatum D1 are activated, they further inhibit GPi (due to the activation of the current inhibitory connections between them). Since by default GPi is tonically inhibiting Thalamus, when activated, Striatum D1 neurons further inhibit GPi. So, the inhibitory effect of GPi on Thalamus is now removed (disinhibition of the connection to Thalamus). Thus, GPi can now send the output (selected action) to Thalamus. This pathway is the **Direct Pathway** and it results in "selecting" actions (often referred as giving a **"Go signal"**).


However, there also has to be another pathway that controls this action selection process to make sure not all available action options are selected. The function of this control pathway is to suppress actions (often referred as a **"No Go signal"**) that have lower salience values, meaning that they are not important or urgent enough to be executed for person to function in the current context or achieve his/her goal. This **Indirect Pathway** works as follows: The input from the cortex (that contains the salience values of actions) also goes to Striatum D2. By default, Striatum D2 inhibits GPe. So when the dopaminergic medium spiny neurons in Striatum D2 are activated, they  inhibit GPe, which in turn further inhibits both STN and GPi. Since GPe has been tonically inhibiting GPi by default, inhibiting GPe results in removing its inhibitory effect on GPi (disinhibiting GPi). This keeps the output "gate" (GPi) closed and so GPi keeps inhibiting Thalamus. Since output of Basal Ganglia cannot be sent from GPi to Thalamus, the unwanted actions are suppressed and not selected.


The third pathway, the **Hyperdirect pathway**, provides the global excitatory effect by sending excitatory input from STN to both GPi and GPe. This pathway is often referred as "**Global No Go signal**". By sending excitatory signal to GPi, it reduces the inhibitory effect on GPi. However, since STN and GPe have a recurrent connection (where in the indirect pathway, GPe inhibits STN) this results in reducing the excitation that STN sends to GPi and GPe. As a result, it reduces the excitatory effect on GPi, making it less active. 

By sending diffuse excitation to GPe and GPi, Hyperdirect pathway reduces the inhibitory effect on GPi by exciting it, and thus make actions more likely to be suppressed if needed. If this pathway does not function, more than one action would have been selected. Since this pathway skips the Striatum and goes straight to STN and then to Globus Pallidus, it prevents early, prematures responses to occur. This pathway also functions as a "safety brake" (another control on direct pathway) if execution of the action selected by direct pathway has to be stopped/cancelled (which can be due to rapid change of strategy or a threat that is not compatible with person's goal or not relevant to what he/she has to do anymore).


The competition between direct and indirect pathways determines whether action/s are going to be selected or supressed (so the one that has a stronger influence on GPi determines what this output nuclei will do). If the direct pathway "wins" the competition, the action with the highest input value (salience value) is selected. If the indirect pathway "wins" the competition, that action will be suppressed/inhibited. Since GPi has inhibitory connection Thalamus by default, the action with the highest salience value (selected action) at the input is going to have the value 0 at the GPi (highest input value is being reduced by the time it comes to GPi level so at the GPi it has the lowest salience value). By this way, the output does not inhibit Thalamus for the action to be selected. As a result, the output is sent to Thalamus.
<!-- #endregion -->

# Modelling Basal Ganglia with Spiking Networks

<!-- #region id="IvwqnJwYksvu" -->
###Nengo Model through Semantic Pointer Architecture


<!-- #endregion -->

<!-- #region id="3f_UgY3s9Zwh" -->
### Definitions:

*   **Symbol:** A symbol is a string that represents a letter/word in the semantic space. Symbols are encoded via semantic pointers (e.g., THOUGHT1, in the model below, is a symbol that is encoded by a multidimensional vector sent from a source as an input to Basal Ganglia).
*   **Semantic pointer:** They are high-dimensional vectors representing symbols (e.g., concepts that are known to us) in the vocabulary.
*   **Vocabulary:** it is a dictionary that contains list of semantic pointers.
*   **Source:** it is the storage for semantic pointer vectors. It can send semantic pointers to the network (e.g., ```MIND``` in the model below is a source).
*   **The "dot product"?** : Taking the dot product of two vectors shows the how similar these two vectors are, the result of this calculation can be thought of as the correlation between these vectors. In this model the dot product happens between the vector representing the symbol in the mind, and the "known" semantic pointers of the symbols in the vocabulary.
*   **Action:** in Nengo a context implies an action. Essentially, it is a cause and effect relationship. The link between these is given by the symbol `-->`. 

The `-->` symbol in ```nengo``` performs an operation that calculates the dot product between the content of the cortex (saliency or "mind") and the semantic pointer for each possible content in the cortical vocabulary.
<!-- #endregion -->

<!-- #region id="Uc0LPl20vd_W" -->
After the selected action by the Basal Ganglia is sent to Thalamus, Thalamus sends this information to "speech" source and makes sure that the associated "effect" for the selected action is presented. An example of a condition would be assigning the "THOUGHT1" symbol in the mind source, which leads to calculating the dot product of that vector in the mind with the known semantic pointer for the symbol "THOUGHT1". The effect of this action would be seeing the "DO1" word in the action source.

The `-->` symbol is the operation calculates the dot product between the vector in the "mind" source and the semantic pointer for each symbol. After the selected action by the Basal Ganglia is sent to Thalamus, the Thalamus relays this information to "speech" and makes sure that the associated "effect" for the selected action is presented. An example of a condition would be assigning the "THOUGHT1" symbol in the mind source, which leads to calculating the dot product of that vector in the mind with the known semantic pointer for the symbol "THOUGHT1". The effect of this action would be seeing the "DO1" word in the action source.

<!-- #endregion -->

<!-- #region id="DBmUxF6KCkbM" -->
### Static Model of Basal Ganglia and Action Selection


<!-- #endregion -->

<!-- #region id="MrpEx9wH043o" -->
We will look at a "static" model of Basal Ganglia in Nengo (not a learning model). We have 2 types of actions. At a given time frame, let's assume that the saliency (utility) value of one of these actions is the highest. When the action with the highest salience (utility) value is selected by the Basal Ganglia and then the Thalamus, the consequence (effect) of the selected action will be executed at the output action module.

The 2 types of input actions are the current states of "HUNGER" and "TIREDNESS". These are represented by the semantic pointers "H" and "T" respectively. If the current state is at "HUNGER" (because it has the highest saliency value at a given time frame), that action is going to be chosen and then the consequence (effect) of that state would be to execute "EAT" action. If "TIREDNESS" is selected, then the consequence of that state would be to execute the action "SLEEP". 

In this model you will see the graphs showing:

1- Saliency (Utility) values of each action

2- Spiking of Neuron group 1 at Striatum D1 (one of the input nuclei of Basal Ganglia)

3- Spiking of Neuron group 1 at GPi (output of Basal Ganglia)

4- Activation level at the output of Thalamus

5- Consequence of the selected action

```python id="1YLsd6zX3X4w"
#Number of dimensions for the Semantic Pointers
dimensions = 32
vocab = spa.Vocabulary(dimensions, pointer_gen=rng)
vocab.populate("H; T; E; S")

#H for Hunger, T for Tiredness, E for Eat, S for Sleep

```

```python id="ExTwBnPabayR"
def state_input(t):                                                             #current state of the mind
    if 0 < t < 0.5:
      return "0"
    elif t < 2:                                                                 #between time 0.5 and 2, action "HUNGER" has the highest salience (utility) value
      return spa.sym.H
    elif t < 4:
      return spa.sym.T                                                          #between time 2 and 4, action "TIREDNESS" has the highest salience (utility) value
    elif t < 6:
      return .5*spa.sym.T+.5*spa.sym.H                                          #between time 4 and 6, both actions are in the mind ("TIREDNESS + HUNGER") and they have the same salience (utility) value                                                          
    else:
      return "0"

```

```python id="ovJaEiT6bcmW"
with spa.Network(seed=0) as model:
    state_input_in = spa.Transcode(state_input, output_vocab=dimensions)
    out = spa.State(dimensions)

    with spa.ActionSelection() as action_sel:
      spa.ifmax(spa.dot(state_input_in, spa.sym.H), spa.sym.E >> out)           #If "HUNGER" input has the highest salience value, that action is selected --> then the action output state is set to "EAT"
      spa.ifmax(spa.dot(state_input_in, spa.sym.T), spa.sym.S >> out)           #If "TIREDNESS" input has the highest salience value, that action is selected --> then the action output state is set to "SLEEP"
     


      bg = spa.BasalGanglia(action_count=2)
      thalamus = spa.Thalamus(action_count=2)
      
    
    p_utility =  nengo.Probe(action_sel.bg.input, synapse=0.01)                    
    p_utility_spikes = nengo.Probe(action_sel.bg.strD1.all_ensembles[1].neurons)#probe of spikes in neuron group 1 (representing the action= Tiredness --> sleep) at Striatum D1          
    p_spikes_bg_output= nengo.Probe(action_sel.bg.gpi.all_ensembles[1].neurons) #probe of spikes in neuron group 1 at GPi

   
    p_thalamus = nengo.Probe(action_sel.thalamus.output, synapse=0.01)
    
    p = nengo.Probe(out.output, synapse= 0.01)
      

```

<!-- #region id="3CImvlOD9k7Z" -->
### Dynamic Model of Basal Ganglia and Action Selection
<!-- #endregion -->

<!-- #region id="cyZ3gs_L8rAb" -->
Here we collect the central *Assumptions* about the Dynamic Model of Basal Ganglia in Nengo:*

**Neurons and Synapses**
- All neuronal populations are represented by LIF neurons.
- Synapses are exponential AMPA and GABA.


**Encoding and Decoding**
- Non-linear encoding via LIF neurons and optimal linear decoding happens for all actions.
- All connections across populations are the identity functions -- this means that the encoded variables at one population are available at the receiving population.


**Semanting Pointers**
- The content of the ```MIND``` is a semantic state, represented by a population vector (i.e., "semantic pointer architecture").
- ```MIND``` is the source of a desire and sends inputs to Basal Ganglia. This can be thought of as the influence of the limbic system onto the associative "cortex". Effectively, a limbic signal is a pattern 'recognized' by the cortex. This input includes information about the current state the ```MIND``` is in. In this computational model, this source includes the 32- dimensional vectors which have the utility values for each action option that you can execute in the current context. 
- There is a 32-dimensional vector representing what is in the mind source. 

**Populations**
- There are 5 ensembles in Basal Ganglia: Striatum D1, D2, STN, GPe, GPi. 
- Action modules are represented by neuron groups in each of these ensembles of Basal Ganglia. There are 3 in the model in this notebook. In each neuron group, there are 100 neurons. *See if you can spot where these are defined*.

**Utility / Dot Product**
- Then there are dot products between → the 32-dimensional vector in the mind source with 32-dimensional semantic pointers for each symbol (THOUGHT1, THOUGHT2). The output of this calculation represents the utility values of concept. 
- The result of these dot products are represented in a 3-dimensional vector in the Basal Ganglia. 
- The 3-dimensional vector represents utility value (distance between) of symbols (semantic vectors) where each dimension of the vector represents the utility value of one symbol. For instance, when the 3-dimensional input vector is sent to STD1, each dimension of it is sent to each of the 2 neuron groups in STD1. So, each neuron ensemble (neuron_group 0, group 1, group 2) encodes 1 dimension of the input vector.
- First dimension refers to the utility value for the first action, THOUGHT 1 --> DO1. Second dimension refers to the utility value for the second action, THOUGHT 2 --> DO2. Third dimension of this vector is the value of 0.5, which shows the condition that there is not a specific THOUGHT in mind. So there is not a semantic pointer selected and no action is executed (0.5 --> action = 0)
- Each group of neurons outputs the dot product of the mind element within the semantic pointer vocabulary. 

**Output**
- Selected action and the other alternative actions in Basal Ganglia are sent to Thalamus. Thalamus increases the value of the selected action more and supresses (reduces the value of) the alternative actions more (this is mutual inhibition). This is to increase the contrast between the outputs of Basal Ganglia that have close values to each other 
- Output of selected action is sent from Thalamus to the "action" source where the effect of the selected action is represented (i.e., if THOUGHT1 is selected, DO1 will be presented in the action source)
<!-- #endregion -->

<!-- #region id="7pptWBT5yPCN" -->
**Mode of Operation**

When we put the semantic pointer value “THOUGHT1” in semantic pointer cloud, we see spiking activity only in neuron group 0, this indicates that each neuron ensemble is trained to encode one symbol (e.g., Striatal D1 neurons_0 encode the dimension that has the utility value of the action for "THOUGHT1")
The training (for excitated groups such as the STD1 and D2) is simply to maximize the output of the representing group, while minimizing the others. And by extension, the other way around for GPi.

- If we assign the "THOUGHT1" symbol to have the highest utility value (by entering the semantic pointer value for THOUGHT1 in the semantic pointer cloud), in STD1,STD2, STN, only neuron_group0 shows activity. But in GPe and GPi, neuron_group0 has the lowest activity because the action with the highest input value is going to be inhibited the most at GPe and GPi due to inhibitory connections. It is even more inhibited at GPi since it receives more inhibitory input as the output nuclei. Since GPi has inhibitory connection to Thalamus by default, the selected action has to have the value 0 (or close to 0) at GPi to not inhibit the Thalamus (minimally inhibit it), so that it can be passed onto Thalamus and then be executed. 
|
<!-- #endregion -->

<!-- #region id="q8IJZma1hiVu" -->
### Exercise: Scenario for the Dynamic Model of Basal Ganglia and Action Selection




<!-- #endregion -->

<!-- #region id="OYXkoiOq90hl" -->
*Scenario*

  Let's assume that we have a thought in our mind. If this thought is chosen by the basal ganglia, we will do the action associated with that thought.

  In this example, you see 2 types of thoughts in mind. If THOUGHT1 is chosen by the Basal Ganglia, the action associated with THOUGHT1 will be executed (i.e., DO1). If THOUGHT2 is chosen, the action associated with THOUGHT2 will be executed (i.e., DO2)

  Let's see what happens in terms of spiking activity of neurons when we apply this scenario:

- 3-dimensional input vector from mind source comes to Basal Ganglia
  
- The utility values of each action in this input vector can be altered by the sliders of node 1 and node 2.
  
- Node 1 slider is used for manipulating the utility value for the first action (THOUGHT1 --> DO1) whereas Node 2 slider manipulates the utility value for second action (THOUGHT2--> DO2)
- Node 3 slider is used for controlling the baseline activity ("0.5 --> action = 0"), which is shown by neuron group 2 activity. By manipulating the activity of this group, we can see how much of the activity in neuron group 0 and 1 is influenced by the baseline activity in neuron group 2.

<!-- #endregion -->

<!-- #region id="s2Fqw4aDcTBl" -->
You can copy this code to a blank document in NengoGUI and run it to see the model, solve the questions and do the exercises!
<!-- #endregion -->

```python id="gzMTmYQLbdIY"
import nengo
import nengo.spa as spa  #Note: nengo.spa used here is an old version of nengo_spa (used in the static model above) so syntax might be different!

D = 32 #number of dimensions of the semantic pointer in mind and action source
model = spa.SPA()
with model:
    model.mind = spa.State(D) #creating 2 states called "mind" representing the cortex, and "action" representing the action output
    model.action = spa.State(D) 
    
    actions = spa.Actions(
        "dot(mind,THOUGHT1) --> action=DO1",   # condition part of the action takes the dot product of semantic pointer in "mind" source with "THOUGHT 1", effect of this is to do "DO1".
        "dot(mind,THOUGHT2) --> action=DO2",
        "0.5 --> action = 0"                   # shows that no action should be executed when there is no selected input
       )
    model.bg = spa.BasalGanglia(actions)
    node1 = nengo.Node([0])                    # creating nodes to manipulate the spiking activity of neurons
    node2 = nengo.Node([0])
    node3 = nengo.Node([0])
    nengo.Connection(node1, model.bg.input[0]) # connection each node to its corresponding action 
    nengo.Connection(node2, model.bg.input[1])
    nengo.Connection(node3, model.bg.input[2])

    model.thalamus = spa.Thalamus(model.bg)    #connecting Thalamus to Basal Ganglia

```

## Tourette Syndrome: Disruptions in Basal Ganglia?

  Perhaps most of you are familiar with Tourette syndrome but did you know that one of its causes is a disruption in Basal Ganglia? 

  Tourette syndrome is a neurological movement disorder that includes involuntary repetitive  movements like "tics". It is thought to result from an abnormal activation of striatal neurons in Basal Ganglia leading to an disinhibition of motor pattern generators connected to Basal Ganglia (Albin & Mink, 2006). 

  Let's see how Basal Ganglia is related for movement in terms of action selection.

Note: You can watch a short video about Tourette syndrome to learn more if you are interested! 
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M8clZP-PI2Y
